thread.title: Apple Rakes In Profits As It Awaits the Next Big Leap

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Apple Rakes In Profits As It Awaits the Next Big Leap
text:
Illustration: Getty Images/iStockphoto By Tiernan Ray May 5, 2018 Is it a good thing or a bad thing if Warren Buffett becomes your top shareholder?
Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway (ticker: BRKA) is almost there with respect to Apple (AAPL), as he indicated to CNBC on Friday morning. Berkshire bought another 75 million shares recently, to hold 240.3 million shares in total, a position of some $44 billion, or about 5% of Apple’s common stock. Apple is expected to be Berkshire’s top position , and the biggest stake it’s ever held in another company, and it puts Berkshire third in line behind Vanguard and BlackRock among Apple holders.
And to judge from Buffett’s glee, he’ll be adding more at some point. “Whatever the earnings are, $60 billion or whatever, and you can put all the products on a dining room table,” the octogenarian CEO told CNBC’s Becky Quick. Apple is an “amazing” company, he declared.
The enthusiasm was certainly good for the stock last week. Combined with a 4.4% pop on Wednesday, following an earnings report from Apple CEO Tim Cook on Tuesday night that beat expectations, the pop from Buffett’s disclosure carried Apple stock to a 13.3% gain for the week, versus the Standard & Poor’s 500’s -0.2%.
Now, given that Buffett used to be the largest holder of IBM (IBM)—a position he said Berkshire has now vacated—this enthusiasm for Apple should give one pause. Buffett’s quixotic tilting at tech in search of something stable is less a tech investment than an appreciation of cash flow. It’s not clear Buffett thinks much about the tech that’s on the dining room table.
Indeed, what’s on the table, while good, represents a kind of stagnation for Apple and the mobile tech industry. The state of tech broadly right now is a bit like the late 1990s, when everyone could sense the ambition and drive to do everything via the internet. The problem was, too much of the technology lagged behind the wildest visions.
Broadband technology wasn’t yet available in most homes to make video watching practical. The mobile internet hadn’t yet arrived, so all internet activity had to occur sitting in front of a computer at home or at the office. It would take another decade for connections and smartphones to make technology ubiquitous so that internet shopping or video watching could take place on a street corner with the tap of one’s finger on a phone screen.
Something similar is under way for the most dramatic fantasies about self-driving cars and the Internet of Things, where every home and city is constantly monitored and controlled. Where every single device down to your headphones interacts with everything else. Where humans live in an augmented reality in which objects in their surroundings react to commands, all overseen by powerful machine learning.
The tech world feels like it’s poised on the edge of its next great leap, but the elements to make that possible are not yet available. Only the dream is there.
The humble reality is that most consumers are sated, not elated, in what they have right now. The smartphone market, the single biggest constituent of consumer tech products by unit sold at nearly 1.5 billion per year, is saturated. Sales for the smartphone industry fell between 2% and 3% in the most recent quarter, depending on whose estimate you use.
Apple’s sales of its iPhone have now missed expectations for two quarters in a row, despite the fact that the latest model, the iPhone X, is the top-selling smartphone in the world for two quarters in a row, according to research firm Strategy Analytics.
The iPhone X is truly a technological marvel as well as a lovely piece of design. The company is well ahead of competitors with its facial recognition feature. But it’s not enough. As this column pointed out recently, people are largely staying with their existing phones for longer periods of time because what’s being offered in the feature set is not sufficiently compelling. ( “Smartphone Growth Sags for Want of Wow,” April 6.)
It’s not Apple’s fault , necessarily. The entire industry struggles with limitations in chips and software that make it hard to advance on various fronts. Intel (INTC) recently fessed up to yet another delay in its shift to chips with the smallest feature sizes as it struggles with manufacturing issues. Rivals such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM), the contract manufacturer that produces chips for Apple and others, has in some ways pulled ahead of Intel.
But in other respects, TSM faces a daunting challenge. Along with the chip division of Samsung Electronics (005930.South Korea) and privately held GlobalFoundries, it is approaching a moment of truth. It must implement equipment technology from ASML Holding (ASML), a Dutch company whose chip-making tools are necessary to get everyone over the hump of the next smallest components, transistors measuring just seven billionths of a meter. Analysts have in recent months been warning that the new chip-making technology could go just fine, or it could produce hiccups in the manufacturing process.
Newsletter Sign-up Without progress against the daunting physics of chip making, everything suffers in terms of battery life and miniaturization to make possible portable devices with increasing intelligence.
Certain enabling technologies have been promised for a while, such as wireless charging, where you can do away with the cable to juice up a phone or another gadget. Apple offers it in a limited fashion for the iPhone X. But a charging pad for the X that was expected, the AirPower, is nowhere to be seen. Technology to charge devices constantly from across the room, has been repeatedly delayed by its biggest advocate, Energous (WATT).
A world of connected devices communicating with one another will require tons and tons more sensor chips, devices that sense light, sound, temperature, and position. There are many promising outfits in that world, including Ams (AMS.switzerland), a decades-old company that has refashioned itself a powerhouse in sensors. Ams’ CEO, Alexander Everke, sat down with Barron’s to show off some of the forthcoming marvels. One is a tiny white cube, just a bit bigger than a pool chalk. It can take measurements of your heart rate just by your placing a finger on its sensor pad. Everke claims it will be as reliable as the typical home heart monitor with the Velcro strap and pump, but obviously more convenient.
Wonders such as this will come, but they will require years to spread to various other devices. And there are too few sensor makers like Ams to supply the goods, and even fewer electronics giants of Apple’s caliber in industrial design.
In fact, an entire refashioning of design and manufacturing is under way to make these new marvels, but at its own slow pace. Design software maker Ansys (ANSS) is rolling out computer programs that let you create what’s called a digital twin, or doppelganger, of any product. Say you ship a car. Once it’s on the road, the manufacturer can get constant input from sensors in the car and model in software how the vehicle is performing on a constant basis. It’s an amazing feat, but also involves a multiyear process of retraining design and manufacturing teams.
Consumers don’t seem to notice the grinding pace at which electronics is moving forward. Staring fixedly into their iPhones as they wander into traffic, they are mostly satisfied with technology’s current plateau.
And that’s good news at the moment for Apple and its suppliers, because it means Wall Street inevitably forgets the problems of the current iPhone and turns with eager anticipation toward the next iPhone. Shares of Apple chip suppliers Qorvo (QRVO), Skyworks Solutions (SWKS), and Universal Display (OLED) all ended last week up sharply despite reporting forecasts for the immediate future that were affected by the smartphone slump. In the fall, there will be growth, for that’s when the next iPhone is expected to arrive.
The current impasse for technology is going to continue to reduce new opportunities for Apple, for competitors such as Samsung, and for suppliers like Qorvo and the rest. But there is enough wealth in the steady supply of what exists to keep investors like Buffett delighted with the cash flow. Milking it, at the moment, triumphs over innovation.
